title: Certify v0.16.0: Part N — circuit-level distances of the Kishony–Fowler colour-code circuit, d = 3 to 15, with checkable proofs — d_circ = 12 at d = 15, where the boundary loss first reaches 3
description: This release adds certificates for the circuit-level distance of the single-auxiliary colour-code syndrome-extraction circuit of Kishony and Fowler (arXiv:2603.28852), built by their own companion code (Classiq/classiq-library a43d3bd4, default schedule, two-qubit depolarising noise after every CNOT, Z-basis memory). For d = 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15 the circuit-level distance is 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 12, for d rounds and for one round, equal to the authors' formula d − ⌊(d+3)/6⌋ at every point. At d = 15, the first distance beyond the authors' numerical range, the formula's loss term equals 3 for the first time, so the value there also tests their argument that the boundary distance is asymptotically reduced by a factor of 5/6. Every value is two-sided: an explicit fault set, checked against the detector-error-model mechanism list that a standard-library script re-derives from the hash-pinned circuit text without Stim, and an LRAT refutation of every smaller fault set, replayed by a standard-library checker that regenerates the propositional formula itself. At d = 15 the 53-million-lemma refutation was also accepted by drat-trim's lrat-check, which read the same proof text. Lower bounds at d ≥ 11 go through the extended code of Strikis, Browne and Beverland (arXiv:2603.05481); the two finite hypotheses that carry the extended-code bound to the circuit are checked on every shipped object, so the route needs a two-paragraph argument rather than the proof of their theorem. The projection hypothesis is the same check that Kornstein makes for bivariate-bicycle cycles (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23394575). Five proofs larger than 50 MB (including the 8.9 GB d = 15 proof) are not stored in git. They are attached to the GitHub release v0.16.0 of github.com/05oz/certify (the two larger than 2 GiB in parts), not to this archive, and REGENERATE.md gives the joining commands, lists the original files' SHA-256 and recreates them from the shipped objects. Credit: the circuit and the formula are Kishony and Fowler's; the extended code is Strikis, Browne and Beverland's; the earliest independent values of this circuit's distance found in the sources read, as of 2026-10-29 (d = 3–9 at d rounds, d = 5–11 at one round), were posted in the qsim-lab repository on 2026-10-04, and our values there are reproductions of them. Two later results concern the same CNOT schedule: Crocker's record doi:10.5281/zenodo.23633600 (2026-10-25) gives extended-code distances 2, 4, 6, 7 at d = 3–9 for the authors' colour rule, by exhaustive search, and Issa and Martonosi (arXiv:2610.33347) give undetected logical errors of d − 1 faults at d = 7, 9 and 11, which are upper bounds; neither ships a proof object for a lower bound on this schedule. At d = 13 the authors state that their formula holds numerically, with no per-d values, round count or method; our value agrees with that statement. Not found in the sources read, as of 2026-10-29: a circuit-level distance for this circuit at d = 15, or any test there of the formula; an independent computation or a checkable proof of its distance at d = 13; or a checkable proof (an LRAT, DRAT or formal proof object) of a lower bound on the circuit distance of any circuit with the authors' schedule, at any d, or of any colour-code syndrome-extraction circuit at d ≥ 11. The nearest items found are Crocker's record doi:10.5281/zenodo.23633600, whose lower bound for another schedule of the same family (C9, circuit distance 8 at d = 9) has a DRAT proof, regenerated from the shipped CNF, for its extended-code step, and the bundle of Shutty's arXiv:2609.21376 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22820614), which ships a re-runnable, Stim-based exhaustive check of its small-instance lower bounds for a different circuit. The dated sweep ships as SWEEP-RECORD-COLORCODE-DCIRC-2026-10-20.md. Not claimed: the other schedules of the authors' table, X-basis memory, other round counts, other noise models. Computations carried out with Claude (Anthropic), directed by the author.
